summary: Describes a framework for defining encryption and checksum mechanisms for Kerberos 5. It creates an abstraction layer between the protocol and the actual algorithms, and defines several mechanisms, some adapted from RFC 1510.

plainLanguage.summary: Kerberos needs locks to protect its secrets. This memo makes the lock slot standard, so different locks can be swapped in without rebuilding the door.

subtitle: The plug-in socket that lets Kerberos 5 swap encryption and checksum algorithms without changing the protocol.

tldr.problem: The Kerberos protocol needs encryption and integrity checks but should not be tied to any one algorithm, and RFC 1510 left the details vague.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3961 defines profiles listing every operation and attribute an encryption or checksum mechanism must supply, a simplified profile built on key derivation, and concrete DES and Triple-DES mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can ask for 'encrypt this with this key and usage number' and leave the algorithm to the etype. The RFC itself warns that the single-DES mechanisms are weak, and it was later updated by RFC 8429.

today: RFC 3961 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8429. It has not been obsoleted, and its own text already calls DES weak.

sections.title: A Framework for Swappable Cryptography
sections.content:
Kerberos encrypts messages of arbitrary size to prove the identities of the parties in an exchange. Nothing in the Kerberos protocol requires a specific algorithm, as long as the algorithm provides certain operations. RFC 3961 specifies the encryption and checksum mechanisms currently defined, and a framework for defining future ones.

Some mechanisms come from RFC 1510, reworked to fit the framework and occasionally corrected where the old text was wrong. New ones are added too. The abstract says the document does NOT indicate which mechanisms are required to implement; that is left to other specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos does not care which lock you use, as long as it can lock and unlock. This memo writes down exactly what a lock must be able to do.

sections.title: Base Keys, Specific Keys and Key Usages
sections.content:
An encryption mechanism must provide confidentiality and integrity of the plaintext, and also non-malleability. A random confounder prepended to the plaintext is recommended, so that it is not possible to tell whether two ciphertexts hide the same plaintext. A checksum mechanism must prove the integrity of a message and preserve its confidentiality if it is not sent in the clear.

Using one key for several purposes is considered unwise, so Kerberos enumerates the different uses of keys and makes a key usage number an input to every operation. Usage numbers are unsigned 32-bit integers, and zero is not permitted. From a base key and a usage number, a mechanism derives a specific key. Other documents should only say something like 'encrypt this octet string using this key and this usage number'. The specific key and cipher state stay implicit.

Each algorithm gets an encryption type (etype) or checksum type number so it can be identified inside the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of using your house key for the front door, the shed and the mailbox, you get a different copy for each job, all made from the one original.

sections.title: The Encryption and Checksum Profiles
sections.content:
An encryption profile lists what a mechanism must define, as mathematical functions with no hidden inputs such as principal names or sequence numbers. Examples are the protocol key format, the specific key structure, the key-generation seed length, string-to-key (a secret string and a salt string, both UTF-8, plus an opaque parameter block), random-to-key, key-derivation, cipher state, encrypt, decrypt and a pseudo-random function.

The encrypt function must include a MAC or checksum if the cipher gives no integrity itself, and should include a confounder. decrypt must verify integrity and, if it fails, return an error and discard the data. The profile also requires that for any plaintext length L1 there is a length L2 with L2 >= L1 and L2 < L1 + 65,536 for which decryption leaves no extra octets at the end.

A checksum profile defines the associated encryption algorithms, a get_mic function and a verify_mic function. The checksum size must be no larger than 65,535 octets. An unkeyed checksum works with any encryption type but should only be used where the checksum itself is protected. Documents defining a new mechanism should describe known weaknesses and include test vectors or other validation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a checklist for lock makers: how to cut a key from a password, how to lock, how to unlock, and how to notice if someone tampered with the box.

sections.title: Key Derivation and the Simplified Profile
sections.content:
Most of the full profile can be filled in from a smaller set of parts for CBC-style ciphers. The RFC recommends that future cryptosystems use this simplified profile or something based on it. Instead of using a protocol key directly, three keys are derived from the base key with a function DK, which applies the cipher to a well-known constant and truncates the result. If the constant is shorter than the cipher block, it is stretched with an n-fold algorithm. The base key is used only for derivation, so one derived key being compromised does not compromise the others.

The ciphertext is the encryption of a confounder, the plaintext and padding, followed by an HMAC of the same data, possibly truncated to h bits. Decryption removes the HMAC, decrypts, and verifies the HMAC. The checksum mechanism simply takes the HMAC of the message under a separate key.

The parameters a new mechanism supplies include the hash H, the HMAC output size, the message block size and the cipher block size, which must be at least 5 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: One master key is used to make separate working keys for locking, signing and checking. If a thief learns one working key, the master key and the others stay safe.

sections.title: The DES and Triple-DES Mechanisms
sections.content:
The single-DES mechanisms are kept for backward compatibility. The text admits that some do not meet all the profile requirements and says new implementations should, whenever possible, use systems that do. The three DES encryption types encrypt a one-block confounder, a checksum, the message and padding using DES in CBC mode: des-cbc-crc (etype 1), des-cbc-md4 (2) and des-cbc-md5 (3). They differ in the checksum (a modified CRC-32, MD4 or MD5) and, for the CRC type, in using the key as the initialization vector. DES keys are eight octets with 56 bits of key data, and weak and semi-weak keys SHALL NOT be used.

Several checksum types are defined for them, including unkeyed ones (crc32, rsa-md4, rsa-md5) and keyed ones such as rsa-md5-des and des-mac. The unkeyed checksums are to be used only with caution, and the CRC-32 is neither keyed nor collision-proof, so its use is not recommended.

The Triple-DES pair, des3-cbc-hmac-sha1-kd (etype 16) and hmac-sha1-des3-kd (checksum type 12), follows the simplified profile with SHA-1, a 160-bit HMAC, a 24-byte protocol key and a 21-byte key-generation seed. Its string-to-key function uses 168-fold of the password and salt, then DK with the constant made from the ASCII string 'kerberos'.
sections.plainLanguage: The old lock (DES) is still described so old doors keep working, but the memo says it is easy to pick. The newer lock (three DES locks stacked, with proper key-making) is the better one here.

sections.title: Assigned Numbers and Registries
sections.content:
Section 8 lists the encryption-type and checksum-type numbers assigned or reserved at the time, including numbers reserved for other specifications such as the AES types, pkinit types and Microsoft types. The numbers are signed 32-bit values. Zero is invalid, negative numbers are reserved for local use, and all standardized values must be positive.

Two IANA registries were created: Kerberos Encryption Type Numbers and Kerberos Checksum Type Numbers. Standards-track specifications get values under Standards Action, and other RFCs after Expert Review. Smaller values are meant for IETF standards-track mechanisms and values of 16777216 and above for others, because smaller numbers encode to fewer octets in the Kerberos ASN.1 encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of lock gets its own number on a list, so everybody knows which lock is meant when they say 'type 16'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that, after advances in large-scale attacks, DES is no longer considered a strong encryption mechanism and Triple-DES is generally preferred despite its poorer performance. It also notes that most Kerberos implementations still had DES as their primary interoperable type. Section 9 repeats that some mechanisms in the document are now considered rather weak for protecting critical data.

The document discusses weak, semi-weak and 48 possibly-weak DES keys, and says CBC mode and the random confounder make the weak-key properties unlikely to be a problem. It describes the CRC-32 used by Kerberos as not collision-proof, with a quirk that makes messages differing only in leading zero bits have the same checksum.

Unkeyed encrypted checksums allow cut-and-paste attacks and chosen-plaintext attacks. A random confounder helps against an attacker using exchanges as an encryption oracle. Reusing the same keys for Kerberos versions 4 and 5 enables a cross-protocol attack, which is why one key should not serve several purposes. The RFC also places no bound on the data handled by one key or operation, so implementations will probably restrict message sizes elsewhere to avoid denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says plainly: the old lock can be broken with enough computers, so use the stronger one, and never use the same key for two different jobs.
